reconcile.connective: Defenders read Hosea 1–3 as a symbolic or visionary commission — not a literal marriage to a practising harlot — so no actual violation of the law against fornication occurs.

discrepancy.connective: Dennis McKinsey argues that if the command was carried out literally, God explicitly ordered Hosea to enter the very union his own law condemns, producing an insoluble moral contradiction.

skeptic.name: Dennis McKinsey
skeptic.attribution: Dennis McKinsey, The Encyclopedia of Biblical Errancy (1995)

excerpts.author: John Gill
excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: It seems best therefore to understand the whole as a parable, and that the prophet, in a parabolical way, is bid to represent the treachery, unfaithfulness, and spiritual adultery of the people of Israel, under the feigned name of an unchaste woman, and of children begotten in fornication; and to show unto them that their case was as if he had taken a woman out of the stews, and her bastards with her; or as if a wife married by him had defiled his bed, and brought him a spurious brood of children.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill identifies the parabolic/symbolic reading of Hosea 1:2 directly, resolving the tension by denying any actual marriage to a harlot took place — the command represents a prophetic illustration, not a literal act prohibited by Torah law.

excerpts.author: Keil & Delitzsch
excerpts.work: Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament
excerpts.attribution: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the OT (1861-75)
excerpts.excerpt_text: The reference to the children of whoredom, along with the wife of whoredom, indicates unquestionably priori, that the divine command did not contemplate an actual and outward marriage, but simply a symbolical representation of the relation in which the idolatrous Israelites were then standing to the Lord their God.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: K&D directly addresses whether the command was literal or symbolic, concluding on textual grounds that it was symbolical — which dissolves the tension between God's command in Hos 1:2 and the Torah's prohibitions on fornication.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the Hosea marriage command as a prophetic sign-act or parabolic representation rather than a literal instruction to commit fornication, resolving the apparent tension with the Mosaic law.
